newsitem.title: ESTONIA: FOCUS-ESTONIA SEEN SEEKING CREDIT RATING THIS YEAR.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ESTONIA SEEN SEEKING CREDIT RATING THIS YEAR.

text.p: Estonia was expected to seek an international country credit rating this year with commercial banks arguing a rating would give the country international credibility and access to cheaper funds.

Previously the Estonian government and central bank had resisted seeking a credit rating as enough foreign funds were flowing into the country with a rating and the government is running a balanced budget with no need for borrowings.
But opposition to such a move has now waned and the central bank, the Bank of Estonia, and the Banking Association are to make a final decision in early May on if and when to seek a rating.
"The central bank supports the idea," central bank governor Vahur Kraft told Reuters in an interview.

"But we need to look at some problems in Estonian such as changing some of the laws to restrict borrowing of local authorities ... and to control the rapid growth of (the commercial banks') loan portfolios.
"If we can diminish these kinds of risks then I think we have a good possibility to go with the commercial banks to seek a credit rating."
Estonia's Finance Minister Mart Opmann also supported the idea in principle -- but not until controls on local government borrowing were in place.
"We have to regulate the external loans taken by local government," Opmann told Reuters.
"After that I do not see any opposition to this idea."
The country's commercial banks are pushing for an international rating with Estonia the last of the three Baltic countries to make such a move.
Union Bank's president Ain Hanschmidt said a rating would be useful but was not essential.
"On one side it seems there is no need for a rating as we have enough money coming into the country but on the other hand this would give certain signs internationally," Hanschmidt told Reuters.
"It somehow makes a difference if you put a stamp on a piece of gold."
Hanschmidt said he expected Estonia would receive a BBB rating if it sought a grade this year.
Olari Taal, chairman of the board of Hoiupank was bullish on the need for a rating.
"Absolutely, we should get a rating," he said.
"The larger banks in Estonia do not have any problems in getting credit, but with a credit rating we can get it at a lower price."
Joakim Helenius, chairman of Hansa Investments, said it was time Estonia applied for rating.
"Although (the government) has no plans to borrow it should leave its options open," Helenius told Reuters.
"We feel strongly that the government should go for a rating because it's not only in the government's own interests but it helps the entire economy.
"Banks and other borrowers on the international markets of course are judged by how the country is rated and given the situation in Estonian overall it should be good for financal housekeeping."
Helenius said he expected Estonia would be able to get an investment grade rating while neighbouring Latvia and Lithuania were slightly below investment grade.
"Estonia should be also to get the lowest but still an investment grade rating," he said.
The prime minister's economic adviser and central bank board member, Ardo Hansson there was resistance to the move.
"This is because of the fact the rating may not be as good as it would have been before (due to the trade deficit)," Hansson said.

"The disadvantage of being small if that you are so much more sensitive to there inward and outwards flows .. and excessive optimism about the Estonian economy is one of the most serious problems we are facing."
He said he would be surprised if Estonia got a better credit rating than Latvia which is graded BBB.
